sq.ANSWER:
Backtracking lets Prolog explore all possible rule matches by reverting to earlier states.
It automatically tries different combinations to find valid solutions.
This makes Prolog ideal for solving search and constraint problems.

Logic programming uses rules and logical inference instead of sequential control flow.
There's no explicit loop or if; control is driven by matching facts and goals.
This leads to a more declarative and concise representation.

lq.ANSWER:
1. Explanation of Structures, Control Flow, and Backtracking (5 marks)

  • Structures in logic programming allow grouping of related data (e.g., disease(name, symptoms)).

  • Control flow is governed by rule matching and logical inference, not by sequential execution.

  • Backtracking is the process by which Prolog automatically retries different rules/facts when a goal fails, allowing it to find all possible solutions.

2. Prolog Program Using Structures and Demonstrating Backtracking (6 marks)

% Facts: disease(Name, [List of symptoms])
disease(flu, [fever, cough, fatigue]).
disease(covid, [fever, cough, loss_of_smell]).
disease(malaria, [fever, chills, sweating]).
disease(cold, [cough, sneezing, sore_throat]).

% Rule to check if a disease has all given symptoms
has_symptoms(Disease, Symptoms) :-
    disease(Disease, SymptomList),
    subset(Symptoms, SymptomList).

% Helper rule to check if all elements of one list are in another
subset([], _).
subset([H|T], List) :-
    member(H, List),
    subset(T, List).
Sample Query
?- has_symptoms(D, [fever, cough]).
D = flu ;
D = covid ;
false.

3. Role of Backtracking and Logic Reasoning in Expert Systems (4 marks)

  • Backtracking allows Prolog to automatically search all paths, useful in diagnosis systems where more than one disease may match the symptoms.

  • It eliminates the need for manually coding loops and checks.

  • Logic reasoning lets systems infer conclusions from rules and facts, making it ideal for decision support systems, recommendation engines, and medical diagnostics.
